articles.title: Why we’re setting up an institute for radically broad thinking
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03397-1The scale of today’s challenges demands a fresh approach — across all disciplines. Here’s how we’re making space for researchers to generate new ideas.
articles.content:
The complex questions confronting humanity demand an interdisciplinary approach. Artificial intelligence, climate change, health and disease, the global economy, migration and the future of democratic societies cannot be understood through the lens of any single discipline.

Why science needs the humanities more than ever

Yet, the need for a broad outlook and the free flow of ideas has become urgent just when the world is facing the headwinds of rising geopolitical tensions, shrinking financial resources and growing barriers to international academic exchange. Today, research and scholarship need more collaboration between nations, not less.

The question is whether our current research structures are adequately equipped for the task at hand. Most academic institutions are organized around departments, disciplines, funding streams and established research agendas, which are essential for organizational coherence but can constrain ideas that do not fit neatly within existing boundaries.

Although many excellent interdisciplinary organizations have been set up around the world — including at our own institutions, which have long championed a culture of transcending borders — most focus on a particular field or research theme and do not necessarily involve people convening physically as a group over sustained periods of time.

The Einstein test: what happens when AI tries to rediscover relativity?

Addressing today’s global challenges at pace demands radical thinking across disciplines — similar to how scientists thought up quantum mechanics, the general theory of relativity and ideas that led to the creation of fields such as behavioural economics, systems biology and artificial intelligence.

This requires throwing open the doors to collaboration, across the entire intellectual spectrum of science, social sciences and the humanities. It also demands forums in which talented collaborators can come together for months at a time.

That’s why our institutions have teamed up to launch the Advanced Research Consortium (ARC), a joint interdisciplinary programme between the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, the Max Planck Society in Munich, Germany, and the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel. Here, we set out how it will work and encourage academics to apply to our programmes in the coming year and beyond.

Freedom to think

Launched on 22 October in Berlin, ARC’s mission is to foster fundamental, curiosity-driven research by providing the conditions for promising collaborations to do their most innovative work and get their most important ideas off the ground.

Scholars from science, social sciences and the humanities will physically gather in working groups and put aside their day-to-day responsibilities to pursue ambitious questions of their choice that might breach conventional disciplinary and intellectual boundaries. The main requirement is collaboration.

ARC will be housed in the historic Otto-Warburg-Haus, which was built for that Nobel laureate, and scholars will be housed nearby.

Physicists honed quantum theory during discussions at the 1927 Solvay Conference in Brussels.Credit: Science History Images/Alamy

The consortium will have neither permanent faculty members nor a predefined research agenda. Rather than asking researchers to fit their questions into an existing institutional structure, the structure will form around their ideas. Thus, the consortium’s trajectory will be continually renewed by its participants and the questions they raise.

This flexible, open rubric will offer scholars from around the world time and freedom to pursue truly ambitious research that might not have had the chance to take root in conventional academic settings.

The objective is not to offer researchers new sabbatical opportunities, nor simply to bring outstanding scholars into the same building. Rather, it is to temporarily relocate them from the day-to-day demands of their usual occupations, placing them in proximity to other exceptional minds, with no requirements of output other than pursuing their most ambitious collaboration.

We cannot — and should not — prescribe in advance what the outcomes will be. They might be discoveries, innovative methods, unexpected collaborations, entirely new questions or ideas, the significance of which might become apparent only years later.

Invest in the unknown

ARC will roll out its programmes over the coming year. Collaborative research will be pursued under two programmes, to accommodate various stages of intellectual exploration. The Exploratory Programs will bring together small groups of up to six researchers for up to four weeks. These intensive encounters will allow scholars to propose and flesh out emerging ideas and determine whether a question merits deeper investigation. The Core Programs will support longer-term collaborations lasting up to one year, with as many as 20 researchers at any given time.

Beyond the collaborative programmes, we felt it was also important to offer postdoctoral fellowships, to provide early-career scientists with lifelong connections and possibilities for collaboration that could shape the trajectory of their research. The Postdoctoral Fellowship Program will support up to ten researchers annually, each for four years, supplying full postdoc salaries. The fellows will divide their time between two of the three founding institutions. As ARC grows, extra programmes might be developed to support new forms of collaboration.

ARC will fully fund participants throughout their residencies in Berlin. The consortium is financially backed by its three founding institutions, each of which has committed its share of funds to establish ARC. As the partnership develops, support from philanthropy will be essential to funding more research projects.

articles.personality_title: New global institute launched to boost big-picture thinking across sciences and humanities
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Today’s big problems like climate change, artificial intelligence, and social issues are so complex that no single field of study can solve them alone. But most universities and research centers are organized by specific subjects, which can limit how ideas grow and connect.

**What happened** – Three leading research institutions from the US, Germany, and Israel have joined forces to start the Advanced Research Consortium (ARC). Launched in October 2026, ARC invites scientists, social scientists, and humanities scholars to work together in Berlin. They will live and collaborate for weeks or months at a time, focusing on new ideas that cross traditional academic boundaries.

**Impact** – ARC is unique because it doesn’t have fixed departments or research goals. Instead, the research direction comes from the scholars themselves, encouraging fresh, daring questions and teamwork. This setup gives researchers the freedom and time to explore ideas that might not fit into usual academic rules. It could lead to important discoveries or new ways of thinking that take years to fully show their value.

**What’s next step** – Starting next year, ARC will run two main programs: short four-week sessions for small groups to test new ideas, and longer one-year projects for bigger teams to dive deep. It will also offer postdoctoral fellowships for young researchers to build lasting partnerships. Funding comes from the founding institutions, and they hope to attract more support to expand the work.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The Advanced Research Consortium creates a new space where experts from many fields can freely team up to explore bold ideas that might shape the future of science and society.

Ce cadre offre aux chercheurs le temps et la liberté d’explorer des idées qui ne rentreraient pas dans les règles académiques habituelles. **Phrase clé** – Le Consortium de Recherche Avancée crée un nouvel espace où des experts de plusieurs domaines peuvent librement collaborer pour explorer des idées audacieuses susceptibles de façonner l’avenir de la science et de la société.

articles.title: What tech entrepreneurs can teach scientists about failure
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03485-2Start-up founders routinely talk about their failed companies. Academia could learn from them, says Mary Ryan.
articles.content:
Stephen Webster 00:05

I’m Dr. Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

And in episode three of Failure in Science, a podcast series about how to do science better, we explore failure and institutions.

Yes, we all have our personal failures, our bad times.

But what if it is actually our institutions that are failing us?

What if a rigid system of education is stifling our imagination?

What if the hunt for grants makes us play safe and narrows our thinking?

Isn’t that failure too?

Jem Woods, who’s a professor at Imperial College London, opened the Failure in Science conference in April with a quote from Albert Einstein:

Jem Woods 01:02

The quote is, “As our circle of knowledge expands, so does the circumference of darkness surrounding it. And we have to continue to keep on thinking around and being critically reflective on that uncertainty and the parameters of that uncertainty and how we perceive what we know and what we don’t know.”

And I think that sits at the heart of the failure in science questions.

Mary Ryan 01:35

Yes, I’m Mary Ryan. I’m the Vice Provost for Research and Enterprise at Imperial College London, and I’m the Armourers and Brasiers’ Chair for material science.

So what would I say my big failures are? When you see someone who’s clearly, you know, a successful academic?

You know, I have a research group at Imperial College, so in some ways, I’ve been very successful.

And I think it’s hard, particularly for early career researchers, to see people who have you know, quotes, “made it,” reflecting that they had failures.

So I think actually it’s really important that we talk about things that we weren’t successful at.

Every academic has got a folder on their computer of proposals that were rejected, papers that were rejected for one reason or other.

That doesn’t mean those ideas weren’t worthy or valuable.

Some of them were before their time.

Some of them weren’t fully developed.

Some of them were bad, and we had to be told they were bad.

But how you respond to that rejection? I think failure and rejection are intimately entwined, right?

And that shapes who you are as a scientist, actually, how, that you get them, but how you respond to them.

But there are many times where you do an experiment with a certain focus, and that experiment itself might fail, or you miss something in the background.

Famously, in the 1980s and early 90s, everybody that was working on surface science STM. Many surface science approaches would use highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG) as a standard substrate.

To make your surface clean, what we did, we’d use a piece of tape. We cleave the surface because graphite cleaves very nicely, as we know.

For about 10 years, literally thousands of people were throwing away bits of graphene on their Sellotape because we were focused on the surface and not what we’d done to clean the surface.

And of course the discovery of graphene using exactly that technique was awarded the Nobel Prize.

And I think that’s just a really interesting reflection that you can be doing a certain piece of work and that is successful, but sometimes you’ve also thrown away what was important.

I think that’s a metaphor for life, probably. By focusing on one thing, you throw away what’s really important.

So at the conference, Professor Jem Woods quoted Einstein’s discussion around the kind of, the circumference of knowledge and what is known and what is not known.

And it’s really challenging from an educational training perspective to get that balance of supporting students to understand what we know, but also understanding that there’s uncertainty at the boundaries of that knowledge.

It’s challenging because that makes assessment more difficult. And there’s a large degree of assessment built into how we teach and train and educate people.

But it’s difficult because it becomes very uncomfortable for both the educator and the student to deal with a space where we just don’t know.

Now, I actually think it’s a brilliant opportunity for thinking about how we design education to really put some of those challenging questions into the hands and minds of students, because I think it’s when there are “What are the big questions of the universe?”

You know, they’ve inspired people for generations. And we’ve still got them.

There’s a danger that we now treat education and knowledge as complete when it’s not. And that means that you’re probably not lighting some of those sparks that we’ve seen before.

I think it’s also really, really important that in a space where knowledge is also increasingly captured and categorized by AI, that there’s a real understanding of people that we train that we don’t have the sum total of knowledge.

We don’t know everything. There’s still uncertainties. There’s still questions.

So you’ve also got to question (when you interact with frontier technology) about what if the knowledge you are being told, what knowledge it has been trained on, what is the boundary of that knowledge as well?

So all of those things mean we have to, I think, bring it further into the centre, what is unknown, before we build on what we do know.

Jem Woods 05:54

So science is founded on experimentation and with the risk of failure fundamentally at its core.

I’m really, curious, I guess, about the balance between applied science and curiosity-driven, sometimes called fundamental science.

And yet, I wonder, aren’t we all curious? And isn’t it that we all want to be curious?

Isn’t that what drives experimentation and testing and knowledge and knowledge generation?

We’re constantly thinking about narrowing our boundaries.

How do we set our boundaries? And yet, we should always be thinking about how we expand our boundaries, how we remain curious.

Mary Ryan 06:37

Professor Jem Woods made an interesting point at the conference around expanding knowledge and this kind, a bit of a tension between discovery, applied science, and how we think about experimentation in that space.

One of the things I like to just try to take everything back to is when you’re thinking about science and applied science, what are the questions you are asking?

Are you asking a why question? Are you asking a what question? Are you asking a how question?

Because that sort of shapes what kind of an experiment you would design and think about.

If you were to take a, you know, a big step back and think about you know pushing the boundary of discovery science, which are often why questions.

And you have a hypothesis or an idea about you know what the answer is to the why, you should always design your experiment to disprove that hypothesis, right?

That’s the way that science actually progresses.

So you should be designing experiments in some ways that fail, right?

Because you’re testing to get to disprove a hypothesis.

I feel like we’ve lost a little bit of that because those experiments are hard to do. They’re hard to think about. They’re hard to publish.

And so what are the mechanisms, by the way, we capture those disproving of hypotheses as really parts of contribution to knowledge.

Because they narrow down what are the right answers and what are the right ways forward.

I still think we need to make sure we capture that as a really fundamental part of the scientific method when we’re doing our training of students.

But quite often, if you want to really, but again, push the boundaries of what you’re going to be able to deliver, you have to work out where those boundaries are, right?

So you have to get to the point where something doesn’t work to understand what does work.

And I think all of those are places where you start to see, and I’m slightly using works and doesn’t work as a failure version, which is not quite the same.

But I think it’s important that you get to the point when you’ve pushed it as far as you can, the frontier of discovery or applied science.

Roseanne 08:40

I’m Roseanne. So I’ve been at Imperial for around four years now.

So I think the failure in education session was very relevant to me because I’ve lived it.

So what I really thought was quite inquisitive was this tension between systemic and individual failure, and how the system might, kind of, create individual failure, but then individual failure can kind of symbolize this systemic failure too.

But I felt that what was really important was to make known to students that failure always carries loads of weight and symbolism within our day-to-day lives, but it doesn’t necessarily mean that we’ve failed.

Mary Ryan 09:17

So during the final plenary session, Rosanne I think, fed back on the failure in education.

And she talked really interestingly about the difference between systemic and individual failures.

Roseanne 09:27

And I feel like the failure in education discussion really symbolized this first step towards acknowledging, number one, that education is kind of underpinned by inequalities.

That means that other people might not have the right science capital or kind of social capital to mean that we all carry the same equal understanding of science, and that means that we need to bridge these gaps.

But also at the same time that we need to fulfill students with confidence to be able to, not fail, but to make mistakes that result in improving and acknowledging that failure isn’t failure as we like to symbolize it, but how it drives you towards creating....

Mary Ryan 10:05

One thing that really resonated with me and what she was talking about was this idea that at an individual level, the impact of failure is not equally felt.

And the likelihood of failure is not equal, depending on your social capital, your background, the disparity that we have in educational inputs, and the disparity that failure or perceived failure has on your educational outputs, and your life chances.

And this is a really big challenge for all of us, I think, to deal with as a society and as an education community, how do we level that playing field on the way in, and make sure that we are enabling the brightest people, wherever they come from, with a background, to be able to have an equal chance of success?

But then also on the other side of that, some people are allowed to fail, and still succeed, right? And we know we all recognize that in life. We all have experiences of that.

One of the things I think this is it really incumbent on educational establishments is to think about building resilience.

Right, building resilience in our students so they don’t feel that a single failure of a single exam is a reflection on the totality of what they bring, on their talent and their knowledge and what they’ve been learning.

That actually, it’s seen as a space for increased learning, a space to reflect and go back and say, “Actually I can do better.”

Of course, we live and our systems, I think it’s where it comes to the systemic part. Our systems are built on a, you know, pass fail first two one.

And I think what we need to reflect a little bit on is how we talk about that.

I mean, I think you know I am I am still a believer that we need to train people to the highest level they can, and we need to say that we are bringing the brightest and the best, and giving them as the best education they can, in order that they can go on and change the world, right?

That’s what we are trying to do.

But how do we say within this pool of people, everybody is valuable, and everybody’s contribution is valuable, and your output is going to go on and make a difference.

I guess thinking about why it’s important that we actually embrace the idea of failure has got many, many different reasons in it within a university and education context.

One is, I think, the perception of what success looks like for an early career researcher.

There is still a lingering, if you start off doing research, the ultimate endpoint view is to be an academic professor.

We know the likelihood of that is probably about 5%.

But also we know they’re not necessarily the most impactful jobs, right?

And so one thing that we’ve been doing at Imperial is establishing a new research institute for early career researchers that helps them see multiple pathways.

So what does it look like to have a job in industry? What does it look like to work in policy? To work in publishing? To work in the public sector?

And then think about what are the steps that might get you to those kind of careers very early on, not as a second choice, but as actually “That’s my north star from day one. This is what I want to do with my research.”

And that’s an important reset on expectations and the expectations that you give yourself and the expectations that we, as an organization, give to early career researchers that are here.

The other area I think is really important is on innovation and entrepreneurship.

Those are inherently areas that are high risk.

They should be high risk, and they should be, you know, we talk about failing fast.

What we also find is that when you’re in an academic culture, students don’t like to fail.

You know, you don’t want to fail an exam, you don’t want to fail a test.

So, what we’ve done with our entrepreneurship for our undergraduate programme, we’ve set that up through an entity we call the Enterprise Lab.

We have programmes that train students to think about entrepreneurship, how to bring an idea and turn it into a device or a company.

We link them to entrepreneurs outside of the university.

We’ve got some mentors for them.

We run many programmes and competitions.

All of that is deliberately extracurricular, right? So it’s not counted for credit.

They can come in, they can explore their ideas. They can be stupid ideas. They can be brilliant ideas.

But they’re not in a framework where someone’s going to give them an A or a B or a C. They’re going to say, “Did I make a company? Did I not make a company? Did I decide I want to do that? I didn’t want to do that.”

And so it completely changes the culture of how they. Approach that activity, and that’s really important for it to be almost like a safe space to fail.

Or almost a place where failing is one of the positive outcomes because you’ve done something that was disruptive and it didn’t work, and that’s a good outcome.

And now you take that and you take it back to somewhere else.

So creating that culture of, you know, have an idea, try something, fail fast. No consequences other than you learnt something, right?

It’s a really important part of how we think about entrepreneurship.

What are the systems questions around innovation spinouts and failure?

People often point to the to the Bay Area, the US, as being this hotbed of innovation, and one of the reasons for that is you can very easily be a serial startup creator, and you have a startup then it fails, and a startup then it fails.

And in fact, when you talk to entrepreneurs in the Bay Area, one of the first things they tell you is the three companies that they had that failed.

That doesn’t preclude them starting a new one and getting funding for it, whereas I think in the UK and probably in Europe in general, there’s more of a requirement for a track record.

So people who have had multiple startups, typically they’ve all succeeded, right?

And so it’s this difference between at a systems level, how you perceive that failure as being “Well, this is my only one chance, so I’ve got to make it work,“ versus, “I’m going to try three or four times until that one works."

We have to shift that dynamic if the rest of the world is going to catch up with what’s happening in the US.

That means a few things. It means probably more venture capital, venture capital is able to take more risk, but also again that resilience in our individuals.

That if this one thing doesn’t work, they should try again and try again.

This has broad positive implications for education and research institutions, encouraging a healthier, more productive scientific culture with potential societal benefits.
articles.personality_title: Scientists learn from tech entrepreneurs: Embracing failure to improve research and education
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists and educators often struggle with how failure is seen in research and learning. Unlike tech entrepreneurs, who openly discuss their failed projects, the academic world tends to hide failures. This can make learning and innovation harder.

**What happened** – At Imperial College London, experts including Mary Ryan and Jem Woods held a conference and podcast series to explore how failure affects science and education. They shared ideas about how academic systems sometimes discourage risk-taking and creativity. For example, students and early researchers often fear failing exams or experiments because failure is seen as a setback rather than a learning step. The university introduced programs like the Enterprise Lab, where students can try business ideas without worrying about grades, encouraging them to “fail fast” and learn.

**Impact** – This approach is important because it changes how people think about failure. Instead of seeing it as a sign of weakness, failure becomes a tool for discovery and growth. The article explains that in places like Silicon Valley, entrepreneurs are encouraged to try many times, even if they fail several startups first. This attitude helps new ideas grow faster. Bringing this mindset to science and education can help students and researchers be more creative, resilient, and open to new paths, not just traditional academic careers.

**What's next step** – Imperial College is working to expand these ideas by supporting early career researchers with more career options beyond just becoming professors. They also want to build stronger support systems so students and scientists feel safe to take risks and learn from mistakes. The hope is that other universities and research institutions will adopt similar programs, making science a more open and innovative field.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Embracing failure like tech entrepreneurs can help scientists and students become more creative, resilient, and successful in research and education.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques apprennent des entrepreneurs : accepter l’échec pour mieux innover
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques et enseignants ont souvent du mal à gérer l’échec dans la recherche et l’apprentissage. Contrairement aux entrepreneurs technologiques qui parlent ouvertement de leurs échecs, le monde académique les cache souvent, ce qui freine l’innovation.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – À l’Imperial College de Londres, des experts comme Mary Ryan et Jem Woods ont organisé une conférence et une série de podcasts pour discuter de l’impact de l’échec en science et éducation. Ils ont montré que le système universitaire décourage parfois la prise de risques et la créativité. Par exemple, les étudiants craignent souvent d’échouer aux examens ou aux expériences, car l’échec est vu comme un obstacle plutôt qu’une étape d’apprentissage. L’université a lancé des programmes comme le Enterprise Lab, où les étudiants peuvent tester des idées d’entreprise sans notes, favorisant ainsi l’échec rapide et l’apprentissage.

**Impact** – Cette approche change la façon de voir l’échec. Au lieu d’un signe de faiblesse, l’échec devient un outil pour découvrir et progresser. L’article explique que dans des lieux comme la Silicon Valley, les entrepreneurs sont encouragés à essayer plusieurs fois, même après plusieurs échecs. Cette mentalité accélère la naissance de nouvelles idées. Apporter cette attitude à la science et à l’éducation aide les étudiants et chercheurs à être plus créatifs, résistants et ouverts à différentes carrières, pas seulement académiques.

**Prochaine étape** – L’Imperial College veut étendre ces idées en soutenant les jeunes chercheurs avec plus d’options de carrière au-delà du professorat. Ils souhaitent aussi créer des systèmes pour que les étudiants et scientifiques prennent des risques en toute sécurité et apprennent de leurs erreurs. L’objectif est que d’autres universités adoptent ces programmes pour rendre la science plus ouverte et innovante.

**En une phrase** – Accepter l’échec comme les entrepreneurs aide scientifiques et étudiants à être plus créatifs, résistants et performants en recherche et éducation.
articles.personality_title_es: Los científicos aprenden de los emprendedores: aceptar el fracaso para innovar mejor
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos y educadores a menudo tienen dificultades para manejar el fracaso en la investigación y el aprendizaje. A diferencia de los emprendedores tecnológicos, que hablan abiertamente sobre sus fracasos, el mundo académico tiende a ocultarlos, lo que dificulta la innovación.

**Qué pasó** – En el Imperial College de Londres, expertos como Mary Ryan y Jem Woods organizaron una conferencia y una serie de podcasts para explorar cómo el fracaso afecta la ciencia y la educación. Mostraron que el sistema universitario a veces desalienta la toma de riesgos y la creatividad. Por ejemplo, los estudiantes temen fallar en exámenes o experimentos porque el fracaso se ve como un obstáculo, no como una oportunidad para aprender. La universidad lanzó programas como el Enterprise Lab, donde los estudiantes pueden probar ideas de negocio sin preocuparse por las notas, fomentando el “fracaso rápido” y el aprendizaje.

**Impacto** – Este enfoque cambia la forma de ver el fracaso. En lugar de ser un signo de debilidad, el fracaso se convierte en una herramienta para descubrir y crecer. El artículo explica que en lugares como Silicon Valley, los emprendedores son alentados a intentarlo varias veces, incluso si fallan en varias startups. Esta mentalidad acelera la creación de nuevas ideas. Llevar esta actitud a la ciencia y la educación puede ayudar a estudiantes e investigadores a ser más creativos, resilientes y abiertos a diferentes caminos profesionales, no solo a carreras académicas.

**Próximo paso** – El Imperial College trabaja para ampliar estas ideas apoyando a los investigadores jóvenes con más opciones de carrera más allá de ser profesores. También quieren crear sistemas de apoyo para que estudiantes y científicos puedan arriesgarse y aprender de sus errores sin miedo. La esperanza es que otras universidades adopten programas similares para hacer la ciencia más abierta e innovadora.

**Una frase clave** – Aceptar el fracaso como los emprendedores ayuda a científicos y estudiantes a ser más creativos, resilientes y exitosos en la investigación y la educación.

articles.title: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
articles.summary: The men and women who rummage through commercial bins to take clothes and other items.
articles.content:
Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket.

On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters.

Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it.

Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come.

During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist.

Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor."
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a grassroots effort by individuals salvaging usable goods from commercial waste, reducing waste and saving money, which has a positive environmental and social impact. The story focuses on a meaningful behavior change with tangible benefits for people and waste reduction, though the scope is more local and community-based rather than large-scale.
articles.personality_title: Local shoppers save hundreds by rescuing discarded goods from supermarket bins
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many stores throw away perfectly usable items like clothes, toys, and household goods, leaving them in dumpsters outside supermarkets. This waste surprises and frustrates people who want to save money and reduce waste.

**What happened** – Darryl Baker, a mother from north London, noticed piles of clothes and other things like scooters and picture frames left near recycling bins. She asked the supermarket staff if she could take these items and was allowed to do so. Over six months, she collected clothes from well-known brands like Ralph Lauren, Nike, and The North Face, saving hundreds of pounds and giving her children new wardrobes.

**Impact** – This small but meaningful action helps reduce waste that would otherwise go to landfill. It also saves money for families who take part. Darryl’s story shows how everyday people can find valuable items in places others overlook and make a difference in their community.

**What's next step** – More people might start asking for permission to take useful items from supermarket bins, encouraging stores to support this practice. It could lead to less waste and more sharing of goods, helping both the environment and families with tight budgets.

**One-sentence takeaway** – By rescuing discarded but usable items from supermarket bins, local shoppers like Darryl save money and reduce waste in their communities.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des acheteurs locaux sauvent des centaines d'euros en récupérant des objets jetés aux poubelles des supermarchés
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreux magasins jettent des objets encore utilisables comme des vêtements, des jouets et des articles ménagers dans des poubelles près des supermarchés. Ce gaspillage étonne et dérange ceux qui veulent économiser et réduire les déchets.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Darryl Baker, mère de famille au nord de Londres, a remarqué des piles de vêtements et d'autres objets comme des trottinettes et des cadres photo laissés près des poubelles de recyclage. Elle a demandé la permission au personnel du supermarché de prendre ces objets, ce qui lui a été accordé. En six mois, elle a récupéré des vêtements de marques célèbres comme Ralph Lauren, Nike et The North Face, économisant des centaines d'euros et renouvelant la garde-robe de ses enfants.

**Impact** – Cette action simple aide à réduire les déchets qui seraient autrement jetés. Elle permet aussi aux familles de faire des économies. L’histoire de Darryl montre comment des personnes ordinaires peuvent trouver des objets précieux là où d’autres ne regardent pas et aider leur communauté.

**Prochaine étape** – Plus de personnes pourraient demander la permission de récupérer des objets utiles dans les poubelles des supermarchés, encourageant les magasins à soutenir cette pratique. Cela pourrait réduire encore plus les déchets et favoriser le partage, aidant à la fois l’environnement et les familles.

**Résumé en une phrase** – En récupérant des objets encore utilisables dans les poubelles des supermarchés, des acheteurs locaux comme Darryl économisent de l’argent et réduisent les déchets dans leurs communautés.
articles.personality_title_es: Compradores locales ahorran cientos de libras rescatando objetos desechados en contenedores de supermercados
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas tiendas tiran objetos que aún se pueden usar, como ropa, juguetes y artículos para el hogar, en contenedores cerca de los supermercados. Este desperdicio sorprende y molesta a quienes quieren ahorrar dinero y reducir basura.

**Qué pasó** – Darryl Baker, una madre del norte de Londres, vio montones de ropa y otros objetos como scooters y marcos de fotos junto a los contenedores de reciclaje. Preguntó al personal del supermercado si podía llevarse esos objetos y le dieron permiso. En seis meses, recogió ropa de marcas conocidas como Ralph Lauren, Nike y The North Face, ahorrando cientos de libras y renovando el armario de sus hijos.

**Impacto** – Esta acción sencilla ayuda a reducir la basura que de otra forma se tiraría. También permite que familias ahorren dinero. La historia de Darryl muestra cómo personas comunes pueden encontrar objetos valiosos donde otros no miran y ayudar a su comunidad.

**Próximo paso** – Más personas podrían pedir permiso para llevarse objetos útiles de los contenedores de supermercados, animando a las tiendas a apoyar esta práctica. Esto podría reducir más la basura y fomentar el compartir, beneficiando al medio ambiente y a las familias.

**Resumen en una frase** – Rescatando objetos aún útiles de los contenedores de supermercados, compradores locales como Darryl ahorran dinero y reducen basura en sus comunidades.
